_about: Mechanical writing rules for every surface that publishes prose. One file feeds the deterministic gates (orchestrator/word_bank.py, orchestrator/prose_gate.py, orchestrator/site_copy_lint.py) and the prompt text the writers see, so a rule is never enforced without being stated. Taste stays in data/ramsay/mindpattern/voice.md. Each lexicon entry needs an example its pattern matches; an entry can add a counterexample it must not match, the models it targets, when it was measured, and a review_by date. Tells drift between model versions (research 2026-10-02), so review_by is when to re-measure it.

lexicon.instead: name the actor and the plain verb: "Kilo Code released 7.4.23 on August 20", "support is in 2.1.239", "the paper went up August 21"
lexicon.example: Stable core v7.4.23 landed August 20.
lexicon.note: 61 uses across all 10 August issues, 165 across 133 site stories. The owner banned it outright on 2026-08-23, in every construction: "this week X landed", "it landed like this", "where this landed for me".

lexicon.instead: give both dates and say what actually connects them, or drop the link. Two things happening in one week is a coincidence until you name the mechanism.
lexicon.example: It lands the same week Ptacek argued agents killed the TUI excuse.
lexicon.note: 18 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: say which kind of quiet and the news comes back: "with no blog post", "in a changelog line nobody linked", "without a version bump"
lexicon.example: A billing bug quietly charged you twice per turn.
lexicon.note: 22 uses across 9 of 10 issues. It claims the writer was watching when nobody else was, which is a pose, not a fact.

lexicon.instead: "released", "published", "posted"
lexicon.example: OpenAI dropped a new model on Tuesday.
lexicon.note: Release-announcement sense only. "Latency dropped 40%" is untouched.

lexicon.instead: use the verb for what actually happened: released, merged, tagged, published, enabled, exposed
lexicon.example: They shipped it Tuesday.
lexicon.note: 202 uses across all 10 issues. It is also the main replacement for "landed", so it needs a ceiling or it becomes the next tic.

lexicon.instead: match the verb to the number. A repo "has 290 points", a score "reached 74.2", revenue "passed $4M".
lexicon.example: It hit 290 points on HN.
lexicon.note: 50 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: pick one plain construction per kind of number and repeat it. Repetition of a plain shape reads as house style; rotating through synonyms reads as a thesaurus.
lexicon.example: It crossed 4,000 stars.
lexicon.note: 99 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: name the mechanism instead of grading it. "Preview-URL coverage is the part that closes the leak" becomes "Preview URLs were the leak; covering them closes it."
lexicon.example: Preview-URL coverage is the part that closes the real leak.
lexicon.note: 45 uses across all 10 issues, the most repeated frame in the corpus.

lexicon.instead: end the sentence at the fact and start a new one that names what follows from it.
lexicon.example: Direct trace reuse gets worse as traces grow, which is exactly backwards.
lexicon.note: 16 uses across 8 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: show the thing that makes it interesting and delete the adjective. If the reader needs to be told it is interesting, it is not.
lexicon.example: The combination is the interesting part.
lexicon.note: 7 uses across 7 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: state the claim without the truth-modifier. "Local-first memory is the real pitch" becomes "The pitch is local-first memory."
lexicon.example: Local-first memory is the real pitch here.
lexicon.note: 39 uses across 38 site stories, plus the newsletter's 35 uses of "the real X".

lexicon.instead: name the concession instead of grading it. "which is the honest caveat" becomes "Google concedes the CPU latency is single-threaded."
lexicon.example: Google quotes single-threaded latency, which is the honest caveat.
lexicon.note: 26 uses across all 10 issues. Announcing your own honesty adds none.

lexicon.instead: delete the frame and keep the content, which always survives on its own.
lexicon.example: The claim that matters: a clean pipeline no longer costs capability.
lexicon.note: 7 uses across 6 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: delete it and start on the sentence that follows.
lexicon.example: Here's the thing: the router never sees the second call.
lexicon.note: Throat-clearing. voice.md already banned it in spirit and nothing checked.

lexicon.instead: delete the predicate noun and state what the thing does. "The model is the bottleneck" becomes "The model caps throughput at 40 tokens a second."
lexicon.example: The eval harness is the mechanism nobody looks at.
lexicon.note: 110 uses across all 10 issues once every abstract noun is counted.

lexicon.instead: split it. The fact keeps the main clause, the verdict gets its own sentence with a real subject.
lexicon.example: It caches the schema, which is the whole trick.
lexicon.note: 104 uses across all 10 issues. The appraisal tag that survived the em-dash ban by moving onto a comma.

lexicon.instead: cut the gavel sentence, or replace it with the fact that earned the verdict.
lexicon.example: That's the whole argument.
lexicon.note: 39 uses across 8 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: name the arguer and use a real verb, or describe what the product does. "The pitch is speed" becomes "Vercel says builds finish in half the time."
lexicon.example: The argument is that context beats parameters.
lexicon.note: 21 uses across 8 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: state the second half only. The first half is a strawman you wrote so you could knock it down.
lexicon.example: This is not just a wrapper, it's a runtime.
lexicon.note: In voice.md and site_copy_lint since March, never checked on the newsletter.

lexicon.instead: state the full instruction and let a second sentence say what the naive version misses.
lexicon.example: Measure the session, not just the output.
lexicon.note: 15 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: say what it is about, in one clause.
lexicon.example: This is less about speed than about who owns the context.
lexicon.note: The em-dash-free descendant of the same reveal move.

lexicon.instead: ask whether anyone actually held the retracted reading. If not, delete the clause and state the fact positively.
lexicon.example: It is a scheduler, not a runtime.
lexicon.note: 132 uses across all 10 issues, 784 across 441 site stories.

lexicon.instead: end the sentence and start a new one, or name the swap directly.
lexicon.example: It caches the plan rather than the result.
lexicon.note: 226 uses across all 10 issues, the highest-volume frame measured.

lexicon.instead: same fix as "rather than": split into two sentences, or name the swap once.
lexicon.example: It streams tokens instead of buffering the response.
lexicon.note: 103 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: lead with the true half and drop the strawman.
lexicon.example: The bottleneck isn't the model, it's the retrieval step.
lexicon.note: 10 uses across 6 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: say which number is the claim and which is the control, which "versus" hides.
lexicon.example: 74.2 versus 68.1 on the same suite.
lexicon.note: 66 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: delete it. If the adjective then feels too weak, the adjective was wrong, so replace it with the measurement.
lexicon.example: That's a genuinely better division of labor.
lexicon.note: 21 uses across 7 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: delete the word. "what the code actually does" becomes "what the code does". If it is marking a contrast, name the contrast.
lexicon.example: It steers the agent away from what the code actually does.
lexicon.note: 79 uses of "actually" across all 10 issues, most in this frame. Banned on long-form only: in a first-person post "might actually fix it" is speech, so social gets a cap instead.

lexicon.instead: once a post is voice. Twice is a verbal tic, so cut the weaker one or name the contrast it was gesturing at.
lexicon.example: It might actually fix the thing.
lexicon.note: Short posts get one use. The long-form ban is stricter because the newsletter uses it as an analytical hinge, not as speech.

lexicon.instead: delete the frame and state the thing.
lexicon.example: Worth noting that the limit resets at midnight UTC.
lexicon.note: In voice.md as a banned phrase since March, never checked anywhere.

lexicon.instead: if the source stated the figure, use it exactly. If you are rounding, say the real number and round in the reader's head.
lexicon.example: Roughly 40% of the calls time out.
lexicon.note: 101 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: keep it only when the thing it contrasts with is named in the same sentence. Otherwise delete "actual".
lexicon.example: The actual cost is in the retry loop.
lexicon.note: 29 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: name the mechanism and stop. "The mechanic worth stealing is self-verification" becomes "It re-runs its own check before returning."
lexicon.example: Steal that even if you never install this.
lexicon.note: 19 uses across all 10 issues. Security senses (stealing credentials) are exempt.

lexicon.pattern: (?im)(?:^|(?<=[.!?]\s))(?:What (?:to do|you can do|I'?d(?: actually)? do)[^:\n]{0,40}|Practical advice|The (?:audit|move|thing|action|fix) to [^:\n]{0,30}):
lexicon.instead: delete the label and the colon, then write the advice as a plain sentence.
lexicon.example: What to do with this: pin your agent version before Friday.
lexicon.note: 10 uses across 6 of 10 issues. The colon label announces advice instead of giving it.

lexicon.instead: make a prediction with a subject and a stake, or stop on the last fact.
lexicon.example: Worth watching whether the fee survives Q4.
lexicon.note: 185 uses across 180 site stories.

lexicon.instead: delete the appraisal and let the mechanism carry it. "The part worth copying is the retry" becomes "It retries once on a 429, then gives up."
lexicon.example: Two details worth copying here.
lexicon.note: 52 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: give the imperative and the mechanism in one move.
lexicon.example: The number to track is p99, not the mean.
lexicon.note: 13 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: lead with the fact and let the reader recognise themselves in it.
lexicon.example: If you run agents in CI, this changes your budget.
lexicon.note: 121 uses across all 10 issues, and 48 of them are the closing sentence of a story.

lexicon.instead: report where the problem actually sat and let the reader draw the inspection for themselves.
lexicon.example: Check your config before the next deploy.
lexicon.note: 22 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: delete "own" unless the sentence names what it is being contrasted against.
lexicon.example: Run it against your own corpus first.
lexicon.note: 39 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.pattern: (?m)^(?:\*\*)?(?:What to do\b|What I'?d do\b|Do this today\b|Here'?s what I'?d\b|My honest read\b|The (?:strategic|honest|uncomfortable) (?:read|part|framing|question)\b|Action item\b)
lexicon.instead: delete the label and start on the instruction or the uncertainty itself.
lexicon.example: My honest read is that nobody has measured this.
lexicon.note: 26 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: one counter maximum, and only when the number carries a claim. If the thread matters, read it and name the disagreement.
lexicon.example: It has 290 points and 118 comments.
lexicon.note: 32 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: one counter, and only when it supports the claim the sentence is making.
lexicon.example: The repo has 4,100 stars and 260 forks.
lexicon.note: 11 uses across 5 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: the cap is on the sentence shape, never on the numbers. Both figures stay; vary how you attach them.
lexicon.example: Accuracy went from 68.1 to 74.2.
lexicon.note: 63 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: name the dates, and name the reason the items count as independent evidence.
lexicon.example: Both shipped in the same week.
lexicon.note: 32 uses across 9 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: lead with what the repo does. Use velocity only when it is the claim.
lexicon.example: It added 2,221 stars in a day.
lexicon.note: 26 uses across 8 of 10 issues.

lexicon.term: the same thing from different directions
lexicon.instead: show the convergence instead of asserting it. Name each source, name the shared claim, and let the reader see them agree.
lexicon.example: Three results say the same thing from completely different directions.
lexicon.note: 8 uses across 6 of 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: cut the announcement and put the facts next to each other. If two findings agree, the reader sees it without being told.
lexicon.example: Three separate results point at the same week.
lexicon.note: 20 uses across all 10 issues.

lexicon.instead: cite the event's own source and date. A site reader has never seen the newsletter, so "the August 17 briefing" points at nothing they can open.
lexicon.example: The decline is worth flagging from the August 17 briefing.
lexicon.note: 160 uses across 150 of 661 site stories, zero legitimate. The site story cites the internal newsletter as though it were a public source. Same class of leak as the internal_machinery lint already catches for "pipeline" and "evidence pack".

lexicon.instead: one trailing attribution per story, and only when the source is a named outlet or a person. "per the paper" and "per the repo" name no locator, so give the figure and the link instead.
lexicon.example: Throughput tripled, per the paper.
lexicon.note: 827 uses across 542 of 661 site stories, 162 of them the locator-free "per the paper" or "per the repo".

lexicon.instead: put the subject in the sentence that makes the claim and delete the verdict sentence.
lexicon.example: That's a real change in how the router behaves.
lexicon.note: 354 uses, including 708 sentence openings across 661 site stories that begin on a bare backward demonstrative.

lexicon.instead: name what made you look twice.
lexicon.example: The thing I keep coming back to is the eval gap.
lexicon.note: Listed in voice.md as an overused tic, never checked.

lexicon.instead: say what you did next. "I read the diff" beats "here's what caught me".
lexicon.example: Here's what caught me.
lexicon.note: The brand line is "a builder sharing what caught their attention", so every writer opens with it. Once a post is voice, twice is a template.

lexicon.instead: give the lesson without the count. Agent counts are pipeline flexing, which voice.md already bans as a credibility move.
lexicon.example: I run 13 research agents every morning.
lexicon.note: 46 uses across 46 posts.

lexicon.instead: say what changes and for whom: "teams on the free tier lose CSV export on November 1"
lexicon.example: This matters for anyone shipping agents.
lexicon.counterexample: This matter was settled in court.
lexicon.note: Opus 5.5 writes it at 116x the human rate. Here: 2 uses in 30 September issues, 4 in 438 site stories. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: drop the frame and state the consequence as its own sentence
lexicon.example: The release matters because it removes the rate cap.
lexicon.note: 29 uses in 438 site stories (3.1 per 10k words), 2 in 30 issues. Opus 5 at 132x human. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: state the consequence instead of announcing that one is coming
lexicon.example: Here is why the new runtime matters.
lexicon.counterexample: **Why it matters:** the export cap is gone.
lexicon.note: 3 uses in 30 issues. Opus 5.5 at 92x human. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md. The bold "**Why it matters:**" label that prompts/synthesis-pass2.md asks for is a section label, not prose, so the pattern skips it.

lexicon.instead: show the stake with a number, a date, or who is affected
lexicon.example: Speed matters here.
lexicon.note: 65 uses in 30 issues (2.0 per 10k), 133 in 438 site stories (14.3 per 10k). Cap set between the two. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: say what it does; the contrast with a straw version adds nothing
lexicon.example: It plans the task rather than merely executing it.
lexicon.note: 6 uses in 30 issues. Opus 5 at 160x human. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: state the claim directly
lexicon.example: The model is not simply faster.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Astra writes it at 157x human, so it guards Sol's edits. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.term: more than an X, it's a Y
lexicon.instead: say what it is
lexicon.example: It's more than a chatbot, it's an operating layer.
lexicon.counterexample: It costs more than a dollar, which is fine.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Listed for all model families. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.term: less like a X and more like
lexicon.instead: say what it is like, once
lexicon.example: It feels less like a tool and more like a colleague.
lexicon.counterexample: It looks more like a tool.
lexicon.note: 2 uses in 438 site stories. Opus 5 at 105x human. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: name the choice and who made it
lexicon.example: The choice was deliberate.
lexicon.note: 32 uses in 30 issues (1.0 per 10k). Opus 5 at 26x human. Cap at half the measured rate. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: give the uptime, error rate, or track record instead
lexicon.example: A dependable runtime for agents.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Opus 5.5 at 23x human, Astra at 59x. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: say what it does and let the reader judge
lexicon.example: This can help you ship faster.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Opus 5.5 writes these at 8x to 24x the earlier rate. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: delete it; it addresses a chat user who is not there
lexicon.example: I hope this helps.
lexicon.counterexample: We hope the patch helps users.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Hard ban. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: remove the tool markup and cite the source as a markdown link
lexicon.example: Revenue grew 40% contentReference[oaicite:2].
lexicon.counterexample: The citation is in the footnote.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Must hold before Sol edits copy. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: use is or are
lexicon.example: The release serves as a reminder.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Guards Sol's edits. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: make the consequence its own sentence with a subject
lexicon.example: Usage doubled, highlighting the demand.
lexicon.note: 0 uses here. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.

lexicon.instead: start with the point
lexicon.example: Let's dive in.
lexicon.note: 1 use in 30 issues. Research: ~/Documents/Research/2026-10-02-removing-ai-writing-tells.md.
